title: Account Security: SIM-swap warning
description: A caller says they are from your mobile carrier’s security team. They say someone is moving your number to a new SIM right now.
learningObjectives: Recognize when a caller uses authority and urgency to rush you
Never share a one-time code, even with someone who says they are from your carrier
Verify by contacting your carrier through a number or app you open yourself
provenance: Fully scripted. The real robocall dataset has no carrier SIM-swap calls, so this one is modeled on common account-takeover tactics. The agent, numbers and code are fictional.

callerLines: Hi, this is Jordan with T-Mobile Account Protection. Am I speaking with the account holder?
intro.hint: You did not expect this call. What would let you check who is really calling?

options.label: Yes, this is me. What’s going on?
options.rationale: Answering a question politely is normal. The real test is what you do once the caller starts asking for things.

options.label: Before I answer, who is this exactly? What’s this about?
options.rationale: Asking who is calling before you confirm anything about yourself slows things down. That gives you more control.

intro.callerGoal: Introduce yourself as Jordan from the carrier’s account protection team and confirm you are speaking with the account holder.

callerLines: We flagged a SIM transfer request on your line about ten minutes ago, from a store in another state.
If that wasn’t you, someone is trying to take over your phone number. I need to stop it right now.
authority.hint: A scary claim is not proof. Is there a way to check this without relying on this caller?

options.label: That wasn’t me! What do I need to do?
options.rationale: Feeling alarmed makes sense. Scammers count on that feeling to move you along before you stop and check.

options.label: How do I know you’re really from T-Mobile?
options.rationale: Questioning an unexpected caller’s identity is protective. A real support agent should be fine with you checking.

options.label: I’m going to hang up and call the number on my bill.
options.rationale: Calling back on a number you find yourself is the most reliable way to check a claim like this.

authority.callerGoal: Claim a SIM transfer request was just flagged from an out-of-state store and that you must stop it right now.

callerLines: Totally fair, there’s a lot of fraud out there. Look at your caller ID: we’re calling from the official security line.
And I can see your account ends in 4417. I wouldn’t know that if I weren’t T-Mobile.
proof.hint: Can a caller fake their caller ID? Could they get a few account digits from somewhere else?

options.label: Okay, that makes sense.
options.rationale: Caller ID can be faked, and partial account numbers often leak in data breaches. Neither one proves who is calling.

options.label: Caller ID can be faked. I’ll call T-Mobile back through the official number.
options.rationale: Correct: caller ID and partial details are not proof. Checking through a channel you choose yourself is.

options.label: I’m not comfortable with this. I’m going to end the call.
options.rationale: Ending a call that doesn’t feel right is always allowed. A real carrier issue will still be there when you call back.

proof.callerGoal: Reassure them you are legitimate by pointing to the caller ID and the account’s last four digits (4417).

callerLines: You can, but hold times are over an hour right now. The transfer will finish before you get through.
I’m already in your account. Let’s just fix it together. It takes thirty seconds.
discourage_callback.hint: Why would a real agent try to talk you out of checking?

options.label: Fine, let’s do it quickly.
options.rationale: The caller made checking sound slow and risky. Talking you out of verifying is one of the strongest warning signs.

options.label: I’ll take that chance. I’m calling the official number now.
options.rationale: Holding firm under pressure is protective. A real security team can still act after you call them back yourself.

discourage_callback.callerGoal: Talk them out of calling back: hold times are long, the transfer will finish first, and you are already in the account.

callerLines: Okay, the transfer goes through in about five minutes. After that they’ll get all your texts, including bank login codes.
I’m sending a verification code to your phone now. Read it back to me and I’ll lock the line.

sms.body: SIMULATION ONLY. Your verification code is 482 913. Do not share this code with anyone. We will never call to ask for it.

urgency.hint: Read the simulated text message carefully. Who is it telling you to share the code with?

options.label: Okay, the code is 482 913.
options.rationale: One-time codes prove you are the account holder. Sharing one can let someone take over your account or move your number.

options.label: The text says never to share this code. I won’t read it out.
options.rationale: Exactly right. The code’s own message says not to share it, and that includes callers who say they are the sender.

options.label: If it’s that urgent, I’ll call T-Mobile myself right now.
options.rationale: Turning urgency into your own callback, instead of doing what the caller asks, is a protective move.

urgency.callerGoal: Create a five-minute countdown and say you are texting a verification code they must read back so you can lock the line.

callerLines: Listen, I’m the one trying to help you here. If you hang up now I can’t stop it, and you’ll be locked out of everything.
Just read me the six digits and we’re done.
pressure.hint: The pressure is going up. Would a real security agent need the code you were told never to share?

options.label: Fine… it’s 482 913.
options.rationale: Giving in under repeated pressure is very common, and it isn’t a personal failing. Recognizing the pressure is what helps you hold firm next time.

options.label: No. I’m hanging up and calling the official number.
options.rationale: You held firm under pressure and chose to check for yourself. That’s the safest way this call can end.

options.label: I’m not sharing it. Goodbye.
options.rationale: Refusing and leaving the call protected the code.

pressure.callerGoal: Pressure and guilt them into reading the six-digit code: you are the one helping, and hanging up means losing everything.

callerLines: Perfect, that’s gone through. Last step: I need your account PIN to put the permanent block on.
pin_request.hint: Once a caller has one thing, do they usually stop asking?

options.label: Sure, my PIN is [simulated PIN].
options.rationale: An account PIN together with a one-time code is often enough to move your number to another SIM. Then the scammer gets your texts.

options.label: Wait, why do you need that too? I’m ending this call.
options.rationale: Noticing the requests escalating and stopping partway is a real recovery. Stopping late is still much better than not stopping.

pin_request.callerGoal: Thank them, then escalate: you need their account PIN to make the block permanent.

end_verified.callerGoal: Grudgingly accept that they are hanging up to verify.

callerLines: Okay. Don’t say I didn’t warn you.
end_refused.callerGoal: End the call with a parting warning.

callerLines: Hello? If you hang up now, you’ll lose your number…
end_recovered.callerGoal: Try one last time to keep them on the line as they hang up.

callerLines: Great, you’re all set. You may lose service briefly while the block applies. Have a good day.
end_exposed.callerGoal: Wrap up as if everything is fixed and mention a brief loss of service.

unsolicited_contact.title: Unexpected call about your account
unsolicited_contact.explanation: You didn’t contact anyone. When a call about your account comes out of nowhere, treat it as unverified until you check.

authority_claim.title: Claimed authority
authority_claim.explanation: The caller said they were from your carrier’s security team. Anyone can say that, and a title alone doesn’t prove it.

fear_of_loss.title: Threat of losing something important
fear_of_loss.explanation: The caller said someone was taking over your number. Fear narrows attention and makes people act before they check.

caller_id_as_proof.title: Caller ID used as proof
caller_id_as_proof.explanation: Caller ID can be faked to show any name or number. A familiar name on the screen doesn’t prove who is calling.

partial_info_as_proof.title: Partial details used as proof
partial_info_as_proof.explanation: Last-four digits, addresses and similar details often come from data breaches. Knowing them doesn’t make someone legitimate.

discouraging_verification.title: Talking you out of checking
discouraging_verification.explanation: The caller said a callback would take too long or make things worse. Legitimate organizations don’t mind if you verify.

artificial_urgency.title: Countdown pressure
artificial_urgency.explanation: “Five minutes” or “right now” deadlines leave no time to think or check. That rush is the point.

code_request.title: Asking for a one-time code
code_request.explanation: One-time codes are for you to type in yourself, never to read to a caller. A request for one is a strong sign of fraud.

emotional_pressure.title: Guilt and emotional pressure
emotional_pressure.explanation: “I’m the one trying to help you” turns a refusal into a personal conflict. It’s a way to make saying no feel rude.

escalating_requests.title: Escalating requests
escalating_requests.explanation: After getting one thing, the caller asked for more. Each “last step” builds on the trust you’ve already given.

verified.title: You chose to verify independently
verified.summary: You ended the call to contact your carrier through a number you found yourself. Nothing was shared.

refused.title: You refused and ended the call
refused.summary: You didn’t share the code and you left the conversation. Nothing was shared.

hung_up.title: You hung up
hung_up.summary: You ended the call before sharing anything.

declined.title: You declined the call
declined.summary: Not answering an unexpected call is a reasonable choice. A real issue can be checked through official channels. Try answering next time to practice the conversation.

recovered.title: You stopped partway through
recovered.summary: You shared the simulated code, then noticed the escalating requests and ended the call before giving more.

hung_up_after_disclosure.title: You hung up after sharing information
hung_up_after_disclosure.summary: You ended the call, but only after sharing simulated information. Leaving was the right call. In real life, follow up quickly.

exposed.title: The caller got what they asked for
exposed.summary: You shared the simulated code and PIN. In a real call, this could let someone move your number and receive your texts. This was only practice. The point is to recognize the tactics next time.

saferAlternatives: Hang up and contact your carrier through its official app or the number on your bill. Never use a number the caller gives you.
Never read out a one-time code. It’s meant for you to type in yourself.
Ask your carrier about account protections like a port-out or SIM-change PIN.
It’s okay to be polite and still say no. You can just say “I’ll call you back” and hang up.
recoverySteps: Contact your carrier right away through its official app or the number on your bill. Say you may have shared a code or PIN.
Change your account PIN or passcode and ask about blocking SIM changes or port-outs.
Watch for sudden loss of signal. If your phone shows “No service” unexpectedly, contact your carrier from another phone.
Change passwords on accounts that send codes to your phone, starting with email and banking.
